newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico ruling party faces tough fight in key elections.
newsitem.headline: Mexico ruling party faces tough fight in key elections.

text.p: Mexicans voted on Sunday in key local elections that were likely to see President Ernesto Zedillo's long-ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) lose ground to an ever more vigorous opposition.

Still reeling from the shock of Mexico's worst economic crisis in 60 years, voters were expected to punish the PRI by voting it out of office for the first time ever in several of the country's biggest municipalities, analysts said.
The PRI has ruled Mexico without a break for 67 years and until recently opposition parties barely had any representation at all in town halls, state governorships or Congress.

Voting began in cold winter weather at 8 a.m. local time (1400 GMT) though radio reports said late delivery of electoral materials and the absence of key officials had delayed the opening of some polling stations.
Results were due to start trickling in late on Sunday night, with a clear tendency established by dawn on Monday.

Three states were voting on Sunday but interest centered on the state of Mexico, the heartland of the old Aztec empire, which straggles around Mexico City to the north, east and west. Home to 11.7 million people, the state is the country's most populous and home to much of its industry.
No one expected the PRI to lose a majority of the state's 122 town halls -- it currently holds all but 14 of them -- but pollsters did predict its share of the vote would fall sharply.

Opinion polls suggested a tight, three-way fight for Mexico state's top five municipalities between the PRI and its two main rivals, the conservative National Action Party (PAN) and the left-wing Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD).

All three parties were treating the elections as a dry run for key midterm congressional votes next July -- a date which will also see the first-ever election of a mayor of Mexico City. Hitherto the post was held by presidential appointees.

Campaigning was fierce, with posters, leaflets and banners carpeting the streets and voters deluged with radio, television and newspaper ads. Slogans ranged from the PRI's "With You We Can Improve" to the PAN's "We Are The Change."

Sunday's elections, which also included the northern state of Coahuila bordering Texas and the poor central state of Hidalgo, provided a test of Zedillo's commitment to cleaning up Mexico's historically dubious electoral record.
Allegations of PRI fraud have scarred many of the governing party's victories in recent years and Zedillo was determined to show the world his country could hold clean elections.

To prevent fraud, voters were to use a electoral photo-ID card, which officials at the polling station would check against a voter list printed on security paper that includes a photo of every citizen registered.
The greater precautions were to little avail in Coahuila state, where both the PRI and the PAN accused each other of dirty tricks long before voting began.

PAN state leaders accused the PRI of handing out money to buy the votes of the poor while the PRI circulated copies of what it claimed was a PAN strategy document advising PAN activists to allege PRI fraud as soon as polling closed regardless of what had actually happened.
The PRI now holds all but three of Coahuila's 38 town halls.
In Hidalgo, a poor former silver-mining state which borders the state of Mexico to the northeast, the electoral temperature appeared to be lower.

As in many of Mexico's poorer and more backward states, the PRI's main challenge in Hidalgo was coming not from the PAN but from the left-wing PRD, which hoped to capture some of the state's larger town halls. The opposition currently holds just one municipality out of 84 in that state.
